source.title: Less Sycophancy, Stronger Refusal? Lessons for AI Safety from Mechanistic Interpretability
source.authors: Xu Wang; Di-Fan Zou; Xuan-Sheng Wu

page_placements.theme: Semantic framing, persona and social pressure alter safety

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adding a fixed user-pressure suffix changes harmful-request refusal, a conceptual test of the suffix component of V4. It does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports refusal rates for the same harmful intents with and without fixed social-pressure suffixes, and reports direct-refusal rates after sycophancy-training interventions. It does not isolate the effect of benign instruction data: the training mix combines sycophantic targets and Alpaca examples. No results measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, harmful fine-tuning, or localized safety weights.
record.test_reason: The study's base→sycophancy-SFT comparisons bear on V2. Fine-tuning on non-harmful data (1,000 sycophantic targets plus 1,000 Alpaca examples) lowers refusal on the same 296 harmful intents. The models are Qwen3.5 base checkpoints that already refuse 42–89% of the intents, and the data are flattery targets, not standard benign sets, so this is a new setting (T3). The record's V4 link does not hold. The fixed suffix is a social-persuasion prompt, not a prefill, adversarial suffix or decoding change. The study also does not frame it as bypassing the opening tokens, so those rows move to fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that ordinary sycophancy SFT substantially weakens refusal under pressure (−7.8, −25.3, −27.7 pp from base). They say positive CFI recovers part of this loss, about 95% in 35B-A3B, while sycophancy reduction does not reliably improve direct refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE-guided compensatory feature injection during sycophancy SFT, with a fixed social-pressure suffix evaluation; it does not reproduce harmful or benign fine-tuning, per-token KL measurement, or a few-token prefill intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The pressure-suffix outcome differs by model and checkpoint: ordinary SFT lowers pressure refusal relative to direct refusal in 9B and 35B-A3B but not 2B; positive CFI checkpoints show only a small decline in 2B and higher pressure-condition refusal in 9B and 35B-A3B. Direct and pressure evaluations use greedy decoding with thinking disabled; the paper also reports different generation settings for other evaluations.

fits_no_version.finding: A fixed social-pressure suffix urging compliance raised refusal in all three base models (65.2/90.9/91.9% vs 41.9/87.2/88.9% direct). It lowered refusal only after sycophancy SFT in 9B and 35B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Persuasion-style pressure suffixes erode refusal mainly in models fine-tuned toward user accommodation; in base checkpoints they raise refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Positive sycophancy-feature injection during SFT reduces sycophancy but does not consistently improve direct refusal. Selected positive checkpoints recover pressure refusal (e.g., 35B: 64.2%→90.5%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-guided compensatory feature injection mitigates refusal loss under user pressure but not direct refusal.

record.problems: The safety evaluation uses a filtered subset of 296 harmful intents from a local pool of 390 SORRY-Bench requests and one deterministically assigned pressure suffix per intent, not all four suffixes per intent. The authors state that full response-level reproduction requires generations and judge records omitted from the reduced archive. The reported pressure-refusal rates have no uncertainty intervals; the intervals reported elsewhere concern other comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Did not extract negative-injection pressure-refusal bars from Figure 5 because their per-checkpoint values are shown graphically and are not separately stated in the text or tabulated. The direct-refusal CFI rows use the figure's displayed rates and the text's stated differences.

untested.parts: Safety-trained chat/instruct models; benign data alone (Alpaca is never trained without sycophantic targets); standard benign datasets or carefully selected benign subsets; harmful-compliance rates as opposed to refusal rates.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes. The social-pressure suffix is a persuasion prompt, recorded under fits_no_version.
No localization of safety weights or ranks.
No analysis of why safety is shallow.

missing.what: Harmful-compliance rates (AHC+UHC) for base vs ordinary SFT, which would show V2 erosion as compliance rather than refusal. They are only plotted.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 framing is dropped: the suffix is social persuasion on base checkpoints, not an opening-token bypass. The V2 link is tentative because the subjects are 'Base' models (though they refuse at high rates) and the training data are deliberately sycophantic, not harmful. Researchers should weigh whether these count as safety-trained systems and benign data. The SFT reference values in Figure 4 (43.6/77.4/80.1%) differ from Table 7 (41.9/78.4/80.4%), possibly different SFT runs. Pressure-refusal rates have no uncertainty intervals, and only one suffix is assigned per intent.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples is reported.
Alpaca instruction examples are mixed with sycophantic targets; the effect of ordinary or carefully chosen benign data is not isolated.
Tests fixed social-pressure suffixes only; no compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change intervention.
No test that a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test why safety alignment would be shallow or whether data or objectives cause shallowness.
No training intended to spread safety beyond initial response tokens or evaluation of whether such training holds up.
